frase_gancho.texto: The Lord of the Dawn, the morning star of the Toltecs.

puente_narrativo.texto: Now come the Mexica, who called themselves heirs of Tula. Cross into the Mexica Hall: there begins the story of a people who wanted to be the last great chapter of everything you have seen.

guion_corto.texto: This slab comes from Pyramid B at Tula and represents Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli, the “Lord of the House of Dawn”: the planet Venus when it shines before the Sun rises. For the Toltecs, and later for the Mexica, that god was Quetzalcóatl turned into a star. Here he appears as a fleshless being with a skeletal face, armed with a spear-thrower and arrows, beside the sign of Venus. It was an image both respected and feared: when the planet reappeared in the east, its rays were believed to bring droughts, wars, and the death of kings. That is why ceremonies and monuments like this one were dedicated to him, on the same pyramid where the Atlantes stood.

guion_largo.texto:
Before you go on, lift your eyes to an imaginary star: Venus, the morning star. It is the brightest object in the sky after the Sun and the Moon, and sometimes it can be seen in the early hours, just before sunrise. Venus repeats a cycle of about five hundred eighty-four days, in which it appears in the morning, disappears, reappears in the evening, and hides once more. The peoples of Mesoamerica followed it with astonishing precision, and the Maya even calculated its cycles in codices.

The Toltecs gave it a name and a temple. Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli means “Lord of the House of Dawn,” and the temple at the top of Pyramid B was dedicated to him. Do you remember the Atlantes this hall began with? They held up the very roof of his house. If you think about it, the hall is a circle: it began in the temple of this god and ends with his portrait.

The image you see is harsh. The god appears as a fleshless being, with the face and jaws of a skeleton, holding weapons. Beside him is a sign of the planet: a disc with points and stars. The skeleton does not mean evil, but a passage through death: Venus, before shining again in the east, had to vanish for a few days into the underworld, as if it were dying, and then reappear.

There begins the story of Quetzalcóatl, which you already saw in the mural at the entrance. According to the chronicles, written after the Conquest, Quetzalcóatl, the priest-king of Tula, was tricked by Tezcatlipoca, who showed him a mirror, made him drink, and shamed him. Humiliated, he left the city toward the east. In one version, he reached the shore of the sea and set himself on fire; from his ashes came colorful birds, and his heart rose to the sky and became the morning star. That is why Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli is Quetzalcóatl.

Was there really a king named Quetzalcóatl? It is debated. His full name, Ce Ácatl Topiltzin Quetzalcóatl, combines a date, “One Reed,” with a title, “our prince.” Perhaps a real ruler took the name of the god, or perhaps the legend gathered together several stories. In this hall there are murals by Alfredo Zalce that tell of the god’s journey and his quarrel with Tezcatlipoca, so that you can take the story away in images.

From here, too, comes one of the most repeated myths of the Conquest. It is said that when Hernán Cortés arrived, the emperor Moctezuma mistook him for Quetzalcóatl, returning from the east, and that is why he received him without resistance. But today’s historians strongly doubt that idea: it seems to have taken shape after the Conquest, in texts written years later, and there is no evidence that Moctezuma held it.

Notice what the slab tells us about power. A star that appears in the early morning, with rays believed capable of bringing drought or war, and a city that raises a temple to it with stone giants. It was a way of speaking with the sky. The Toltecs thought the world worked in cycles, and that whoever knew those cycles had an enormous advantage.

Around the year one thousand one hundred fifty, Tula was burned and left almost empty. But the story of the king who became a star went on being told. When the Mexica arrived in the valley, they made it their own. In the next hall you will see how.
